For patients with extrapulmonary small cell cancers, both surgery and radiation therapy have been shown to improve median, 5- and 10-year survival rates. However, it is essential to note that outcomes for EPSCC (extrapulmonary small cell carcinoma) remain poor.

In terms of specific treatments, oncoplastic surgery may be considered for selected low-risk breast cancer patients undergoing radiation therapy, but further investigation is needed to determine its feasibility and potential benefits. Exclusive chemotherapy with radiation (chemoradiation) is not recommended for rectal tumors, and a high-dose radiotherapy approach is not sufficient for palliative lung cancer treatment.

The condition of the cell microenvironment of mediastinal lymph nodes may help predict the risk of metastases in non-small cell lung cancer, but further research is necessary to confirm this approach. Progression of a pT3 renal cell carcinoma is not associated with increased VEGF expression, and chemotherapy has been shown to significantly prolong survival in patients with performance status 1 or less.

Regarding cervical physical therapy for tinnitus in patients with cervicogenic somatic tinnitus, preliminary results suggest that it may have a positive effect on subjective complaints. However, larger studies are necessary to confirm these findings and understand the underlying mechanisms.

Finally, regarding gender differences in survival among resected non-small cell lung cancer patients, women had better survival rates than men. Additionally, there was no survival advantage for men in propensity-matched gender pairs, suggesting that pathobiology may differ between genders in adenocarcinoma.

In summary, both surgery and radiation therapy have been shown to improve survival outcomes for patients with extrapulmonary small cell cancers. Further research is needed to fully understand the potential benefits and risks of these treatments, particularly regarding oncoplastic surgery and chemotherapy with radiation.
